To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the maximum repetition rate of a normal conducting linac is determined by the maximum achievable gradient and by the maximum allowable heat load, which is limited by the maximum allowable surface temperature.

(i) the radiation load in the accelerating structures is the limiting factor for operation in a regime of high repetition rate and (ii) the radiation load is proportional to the square of the accelerating gradient, the square of the repetition rate and to the square of a parameter, the normalized frequency, which characterizes the bunch length and the accelerating structure.

the radiative regime of linear electron–positron accelerators and high repetition rate free electron lasers can be scaled to high energies and high luminosities with the following scalings: (a) the energy of a linear collider can be scaled to a few TeV by increasing the accelerating gradient and the number of bunches in a train, (b) a high energy collider can be operated with a high luminosity by increasing the number of trains and the number of colliding bunches in a collision
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of novel high gradient acceleration structures and the associated beam physics, which are required to achieve high luminosities in future linear colliders and to enable the operation of normal conducting linear accelerators at repetition rates in excess of 1 MHz.
the development of high power microwave (HPM) and millimeter wave (MMW) sources and their applications.
the design and construction of high-gradient accelerating structures and their application to high energy and high repetition rate electron linacs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radiative regime is not a limitation to the performance of linear colliders and high repetition rate free electron lasers.

the present state of the art in the development of accelerating structures for high energy linear colliders is not adequate for the realization of the high energy and luminosity goals set by the International Linear Collider Technical Design Report (ILC TDR).
the present state of the art of the technology is not yet sufficient to allow the construction of a collider with the parameters of CLIC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the high repetition rate operation of linac driven free electron lasers is possible with a normal conducting linac, but that a superconducting linac is necessary for high energy and high intensity linear colliders.
there is no fundamental limitation for normal conducting structures to operate in the highly radiatable regime, provided the structures can be designed and manufactured in an efficient way.

, for a collider, the most promising approach is the use of a normal conducting structure with a gradient of 50 MV/m and an average current of 1.2 A, with the option of a 100 MV/m gradient and 2.4 A average current, for a total length of 2 km.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the scaling of the luminosity of a linear collider in the highly radiatively dominated regime is limited by the accelerating gradient of the structure.
the scaling of high luminosity electron colliders is not limited by the accelerating structure, but rather by the radiation load on the beam screen.
the scaling of the radiative regime is not as simple as it may seem.
